activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Jake wanted to play house. He had a teddy bear, a blanket, and a small cup. But his teddy bear looked sad on the floor.

Jake picked up the teddy bear. He wrapped it in the gray blanket. He held it like a baby. "Time for milk," he said. He tipped the little cup to its mouth. Then he patted its back, soft and slow.

The teddy bear still sat crooked. It kept sliding down. Jake tried again and again. Then he saw why. The blanket was too big. It pushed the bear out of his arms.

Jake folded the blanket in half. Now it was small. He wrapped the bear snug and tight. The bear stayed put in his arms.

"See, Robot?" Jake said to his toy robot on the shelf. "Big blanket made you slip. Small blanket helps you stay." He rocked the bear side to side. The room felt quiet and warm.

Robot watched with his shiny gray eyes. Jake sang a tiny song. "Sleep now, baby bear," he whispered. The bear's head rested on Jake's shoulder.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Austin ran to the big slide at the playground. The sun was hot on his hands. He touched the slide. "Ow! Hot!" said Austin. He could not go down alone.

Dad came with a water bottle. He poured cold water on the slide. Splash! The water ran down, down, down. Austin touched the slide again. Now it felt cold. The hot sun made the slide hot. The cold water made it cool. "Big slide, big splash," said Austin.

Austin climbed up slowly. Then he went down fast. Whee! A little dog ran by the fence. It was small, like a toy horse. "Fast dog, slow me," said Austin. He slid down one more time. Dad held out his arms. Austin landed right in them.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Nova went to her friend Milo's house. It was still early. The sun was just coming up. Nova had brought her baby doll. The doll was small and soft.

"Let's play house," said Milo. Nova held her doll. "The baby is crying," she said. "She needs milk." But Nova had no bottle. Milo looked around the room. He found a yellow block. "This can be the bottle," he said. Nova tipped the block to the doll's mouth. She made little drinking sounds. "There, there," she said softly. The doll went quiet. Nova smiled. "The baby stopped crying because we fed her," she said.

Then Milo put chairs in a row. "This is our bus," he said. "You can drive, Nova. I will hold the baby." Nova sat at the front. She turned a plate for the wheel. The cat crawled under the chairs. It rode on the bus too. "Next stop, the park!" said Nova. Milo laughed and bounced the doll on his lap. "One ticket for the baby, please," he said. "And one fish ticket for the cat."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Liam ran to the toy box at daycare. "Truck!" he shouted. He felt so excited. His tummy jumped like a bunny.

Then Ben grabbed the truck. "My truck!" said Ben. Liam's face got hot. His hands made fists. He was angry. He wanted to push Ben. He stomped his foot. It was very loud.

Miss Rosa came over. "Liam, you look angry," she said. "Big breaths help." She took a big breath in. Liam copied her. He breathed in. He breathed out. His fists opened. His tummy felt slow and calm now. "The big breath made the angry go small," said Liam. "Yes," said Miss Rosa. "You did it all by yourself." She helped him pat Ben's back gently. "Truck please?" asked Liam. Ben smiled. The room was noisy and warm. Liam and Ben rolled the truck on the rug together.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Emile runs into art class. Today he wants to paint a house. A big house with windows!

He dips his round brush in paint. He moves it on the paper. Round and round. The window comes out as a circle. But a circle is round like a ball. House windows are not round like balls.

Emile looks around the table. Nobody is playing with the sponge stamps. He is alone at his spot. He picks up a sponge. It has four flat sides. He taps it in green paint. He presses it on the paper. A square! A window with four flat sides!

He finds a triangle sponge too. Tap, press. A roof! He finds a long rectangle sponge. Tap, press. A door!

"Look, a house!" says Emile. His teacher smiles. She takes out her phone. Click! She took a picture.

Emile points at the circle window. "Round brush makes circles," he says. "Flat sponge makes squares!" He taps the sponge again. One more window goes on the house.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Eva went to the playground with Grandma. The gate was open. Eva ran in fast. "Wait for me," said Grandma. Eva stopped and held Grandma's hand.

Eva wanted to play on the big slide. But the sun was on it. She put her hand near it. The slide was hot. Eva pulled her hand back. "One, two, three," she said. She waited and counted some more. Grandma waited too. Then a cloud came. The slide got cool. Eva touched it. Now it was not hot. She slid down. "The sun made it hot," said Eva. "The cloud made it cool."

Next to the slide, Eva saw a shiny can on the ground. She did not touch it. She asked Grandma to pick it up. Grandma put it in the bin. "Good girl," said Grandma. Eva counted the swings. "One, two, three, four swings." She found a free one and climbed on. "Stay close, Grandma," said Eva. "I will," said Grandma. "I like to watch you fly."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Zoe sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a green leaf for the class tree. But there was no green paint. There was only red, yellow, and blue.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Zoe. She tapped each pot. "Where is green hiding?"

Her brush was polite and waited quietly. Zoe dipped it in yellow. She put yellow on the paper. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. She put blue right on top of the yellow.

Something magic happened. The two colours swirled. They held hands. They turned into green!

"Green!" said Zoe. "Yellow and blue make green!"

She painted a big leaf. Then she painted more. She put leaves all over the paper. The class tree filled up with green.

Tom came to look. "How did you do that?" he asked.

Zoe held up her brush like a magic wand. "Yellow plus blue," she whispered. "That is the secret spell."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Sebastian stood in the backyard. Dad put a hoop on the grass. Dad gave him a small beanbag. Sebastian wanted to make it land inside the hoop.

He threw the beanbag hard. It sailed way over the hoop. It landed in the flowers. Sebastian ran and got it.

He tried again, softer this time. The beanbag went up high. It came down. It dropped right into the circle. Sebastian clapped his hands. "It went up, then it came down in!" he said.

Then Dad rolled him a big ball. Sebastian held his arms out stiff. The ball hit his arms and bounced away. His hands were like hard wood.

Dad rolled the ball again. This time Sebastian let his arms go soft, like a pillow. The ball touched his hands and sat there. He had caught it. "My arms are soft, so the ball stays!" said Sebastian.

Two busy little hands held the big ball all the way to Dad.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Ivy ran to the sandbox on a hot summer day. She had ten little stones in her red cup. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then Ivy jumped. The cup tipped over. The stones went spill, spill, spill into the sand.

"Oh no," said Ivy. "My stones are hiding." A boy named Sam came over. He dug with her, slow and careful.

Ivy picked up stones one by one. "One, two, three," she said. She kept going. "Seven, eight, nine." She looked all around. One stone was still lost. It was under the slide. Sam pointed to it.

"Ten!" said Ivy. "All ten are back. Counting tells me if they are all here."

"Count me too," said Sam, and he laughed.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Olivier dug a little hole. He dropped a seed in. Then he patted the dirt on top. His pink boots squished in the mud.

Papa gave Olivier a watering can. Olivier poured water on his seed. "Will it grow now?" he asked. "Let's wait and see," said Papa.

The next day, Olivier ran to the garden. He saw two spots of dirt. One spot was dark and wet. One spot was dry. Where had he poured the water? The wet spot had a tiny green sprout. The dry spot had nothing at all. "Oh!" said Olivier. "The water helped this one. That dry seed got no drink." He poured water on the dry spot too. He patted the dirt gently, like patting a puppy.

On the way home, Papa gave him a cookie. Olivier munched and wondered, "Will my sprout be big tomorrow?" He looked back one more time. The little green sprout stood up tall, like it was waving goodbye.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Eliana was at Grandma's house. She wanted to read her library book forever. The book had a purple cover and a picture of a bear. On the first page, words sat in a row. "Grandma, what do the words say?" she asked. Grandma turned the pages from front to back. She read every word out loud. The words told about a bear who could crawl under a fence. Words were like magic. They talked without a mouth!

Eliana held the book tight. "This book is mine now," she said. But Grandma pointed at a little paper slip inside. The slip had words on it too. Grandma read the words. The book had to go back to the library. Other kids wanted to read it too.

The next day they drove to the library. Eliana gave the book to the lady at the desk. Then the lady smiled and gave it right back. "You can borrow it again," she said. Eliana hugged the purple book. "It comes back to me!" she said. On the way home, she drew a map to the library, with a big bear on it.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Isaac sat in the waiting room. He held his favorite teddy bear. His father sat right next to him. Today Isaac would get a shot. He did not want a shot. "It might pinch," Isaac said. "I will hold your hand," said his father.

A nurse came in. "Squeeze your bear tight," she said. Isaac squeezed the bear. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." It was done! The shot was very fast. Isaac looked at his arm. There was a small round bandage on it. "The bear helped me," Isaac said. "I squeezed him and it went fast!"

Isaac got a sticker with a star on it. He put it on his shirt. His father picked him up. Isaac waved to the nurse. "The shot is done!" he said. Then he hugged his teddy bear tight.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story: Elena woke up and saw white outside. "Snow! Why is there snow?" She ran to the window. "Because it snowed all night!" School was closed. Mama said, "Let's go play." Elena put on her boots and her big red coat. Outside, the street was quiet and white. She made a snowball. She held it and held it. Then she opened her mitten. "Where did my snowball go?" It was just water! She made another one. Again, it melted in her warm hand. "My hands are warm. Warm hands make snow melt!" She laughed and made one more. She let it sit on the cold sidewalk instead. It stayed a snowball! Down the street, Papa tapped the icicles on the porch. Tap, tap, like a little hammer. An icicle fell down. "Catch it, Elena!" She ran, and the icicle dripped, dripped, dripped in her warm hand. "It's turning to water too!" she shouted. Elena stomped her boots and shouted to the sky, "Warm makes snow melt! Warm makes snow melt!" Mama said hot cocoa was ready. Elena stomped inside, still laughing. The snow stayed out on the cold street. It waited for her.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Matteo woke up when the sky was still dark. "School today," said Mama. Matteo put on his socks. One sock went on his foot. Then the other sock. It took a long time. Mama waited.

Matteo wanted his red truck to come too. "It will not fit in your hand when you paint," said Mama. So Matteo put the truck in his backpack. The zipper went zzzz. The truck was hidden inside. "The backpack holds it," said Matteo. "It is too big for my pocket."

At school, Matteo hung his backpack on a low hook. It was just his size. He painted a big sun. Then he unzipped his backpack. The red truck was still there. "The hook kept my spot," said Matteo. "Truck, we did it."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Jasper had a special red car. He played with it every day. Now the car was gone. "Oh no," said Jasper. He looked and looked.

Miss Maya came to help. "Let's go back where you played," she said. "One, the slide. Two, the sandbox. Three, the big tree." Jasper ran to the slide. No car. He dug in the sandbox. No car. A leaf fell from the big tree. Then he saw something under the leaf. It was his special car!

"The leaf hid it," said Jasper. "The car was there the whole time." Miss Maya smiled. "The car got lost because you left it under the tree," she said. Jasper held the car tight.

Miss Maya had an idea. "Let's fix a pocket for it." She pinned a little pouch on Jasper's shirt. Jasper put the car inside. "Safe now," he said. "One slide, two sandbox, three tree, and my car is home."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
William wanted the red truck. His sister Mia had the red truck. She pushed it fast across the floor.

"Can I have a turn?" William asked. Mia said, "Wait for my turn to end." William sat down on the rug. He watched the truck go. He waited and waited.

Soon Mia said, "My turn is done. Now it is your turn." William held the truck. He pushed it fast. It went all the way to the toy box.

"Your turn lasted long," said Mia. "I counted to ten." William counted too. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. "Turn done!" he said. He gave the truck back to Mia.

Mama called, "Dinner time!" William helped Mia shut the toy box. Then they ran to the table together.

"Your turn, then my turn," said William. "That is fair." Mia smiled and hugged him.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Florence found a pink flower in the backyard. She wanted to tell Grandma all about it. But she forgot the words for it.

"Can you guess the words?" asked Grandma. "Let's count your helpers."

Grandma touched Florence's eyes. "One. Eyes see the flower." Florence looked at the pink petals. "Eyes see!" she said.

Grandma touched her ears. "Two. Ears hear." A bee went buzz. Florence laughed. "Ears hear the bee!"

"Three," said Grandma, touching Florence's nose. "Nose smells." Florence sniffed the flower. It smelled sweet. "Nose smells sweet!"

"Four," said Grandma, and she touched Florence's ears again. Florence shook her head. "No! Ears is two!" Grandma giggled. "You got me! Four is your tongue. Tongue tastes."

"Five," said Florence. She touched her own hands. "Hands touch the flower." She petted one soft petal. "Hands touch soft!"

Then Grandma closed Florence's eyes with her fingers. "No peeking. Guess what this is." Florence sniffed. Sweet. "The flower! My nose knows!"

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Noah ran onto the green grass. It was soccer practice. Coach Maya held one big blue ball. The ball was blue like the ocean.

Tommy got the ball first. Tommy kicked it to the cone. Noah wanted a turn right away. He ran fast and grabbed the ball with both hands. Tommy fell down and started to cry. Coach Maya blew her whistle. Nobody could play now.

"Noah, look," said Coach Maya. She pointed at Tommy. "When you grab, Tommy falls. Then we all stop." Noah looked at Tommy's sad face. Noah felt mad at first. But then he saw why Tommy cried. "I grabbed too hard," Noah said. "That is why you fell."

Coach Maya had a plan. She held up a paper. "We will write the names down," she said. "Tommy first. Then Noah." She wrote both names with her pen. Noah sat on the grass and waited. He counted to ten. Then Tommy kicked the ball and said, "Your turn, Noah!" Noah kicked it all the way to the far cone.

After practice, Coach Maya gave Noah a big hug. "You waited," she said. "That was hard and you did it." Noah smiled and held her hand. "Can we play again tomorrow?" he asked.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Rehmat looked out the kitchen window. Snow was falling on the grass. No school today. "Snow day!" said Mama.

Rehmat was hungry. She wanted warm milk. Mama put snow in a small pot. "We will melt it," said Mama. Rehmat counted the snowballs going in. One snowball. Two snowballs. Three snowballs. Mama put the pot on the hot stove. Rehmat waited. She watched and waited.

The snow began to melt. One snowball got small. Two snowballs got small. Then all the snow turned into water. But it was only a little water. "The snow was mostly air," said Mama. Rehmat looked at the tiny bit of water. "Snow is big, but water is small," she said. They melted more snow, one, two, three, four. At last there was enough. Mama warmed the milk. Rehmat drank it slowly. "Snow made my milk," she said, and smiled.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Charles sat at the dinner table. His toe tapped under his chair. "Pancakes now?" he asked.

Mom shook her head. "Pancakes are tomorrow," she said. "Yesterday we had no eggs. Today I went to the store. I got a tiny carton of eggs."

Charles picked up his fork. He looked at his plate. There was rice and chicken on it. "But I want pancakes today," he said.

"We eat dinner now," said Mom. "Later we can have a pear. Pancakes come after sleeping. Tomorrow means after this night."

Charles took one bite of chicken. Then he took another bite. He thought hard. "So yesterday there were no eggs," he said. "Then today you got eggs. So tomorrow we can make pancakes!"

"That is just right," said Mom. She smiled at him. Dad came and sat in his big chair. He gave Charles a tiny piece of pear.

"Now we eat together," said Dad. Charles picked up the pear with his fingers. He put it in his mouth. It was sweet.

"After I sleep, it will be tomorrow," said Charles. "Then pancakes!" He wiggled his happy toe under the table. Mom kissed the top of his head.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Raphael ran to the toy corner at daycare. His friend Mia was rocking a baby doll. The baby had no blanket. Mia said the baby was cold. Raphael wanted to help the baby.

He looked around. What could be a blanket? He saw a thick sock on the floor. It was big and warm. He put the sock over the baby. "Now the baby is warm," said Raphael. Mia rocked the baby some more. The baby went to sleep.

Then Raphael picked up a small block. He held it like a bottle. He tipped it to the baby's mouth. "Baby is hungry," he said. "The block is the milk." Mia clapped her hands. "A block can be a bottle!" she said.

Raphael wondered what else could turn into something new. He looked at his shoe. Could a shoe be a car? He pushed it across the rug. Vroom, vroom! The shoe was a car now. "Thank you, shoe," said Raphael. "You are my fast car."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
David woke up and looked out the window. The sky had dropped snow all night long. The grass was gone. The road was white. There was no school today. "Snow day," said Mom. David put on his boots.

Dad helped him fish his red sled out of the shed. "Be careful on the big hill," said Dad. David climbed up. He sat down. He pushed off. But the sled went slow, slow, slow. He looked at the ground. The snow was thin here. He could see little bits of grass. David climbed up again. He dragged the sled to the deep, thick snow. He sat down. He pushed off. The sled went fast, fast, fast.

"I know why," said David. "Thick snow makes me go fast. Thin snow makes me go slow." Dad laughed and waved. David climbed the hill one more time. "Here I go," he said.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Elizabeth ran to the swings at the park. There was only one swing left. A boy was already on it.

Elizabeth wanted that swing very much. Her tummy felt tight. She stood still and watched. The boy swung up high, then down low. Then he stopped and got off. He held the swing out to her.

"You waited, so it is your turn," he said.

Elizabeth sat on the swing. "You waited, so it is your turn," she said to herself. That was why she got the swing. She had waited, not pushed.

After swinging, Elizabeth found her mom on a bench. Mom had a small cake with her. It was a round cake with pink icing. "We will share it," said Mom. Mom cut the cake into two equal pieces. One for Elizabeth, one for Mom. The pieces were the same size. That is what fair means, Elizabeth thought.

A little girl came by. She looked at the cake. Elizabeth looked at her one piece. Then she looked at the girl. Elizabeth broke her piece in two.

"This half is for you," Elizabeth said.

The girl smiled big. She sat down next to Mom on the bench.

"Thank you," said the girl. "I have cookies. You can have one."

Elizabeth took the cookie. It was round like the cake. She bit it, and it was sweet.

"Sharing makes more, not less," said Mom.

Elizabeth ate her cake. The sun was warm. Mom held her hand. The swing went back and forth, all by itself.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Emily sat in her car seat. Her tummy made a big growl. "I want a snack," she said.

Daddy played a game. "Guess what is in the bag," he said. He knocked on the bag, tap tap. Emily giggled. "A cow?" she asked. "No, a cow is an animal. It says moo." Daddy opened the bag. "It is a banana. A banana is food. You can eat it!"

Emily took a bite. Yum. Then she saw something on the window. "A spider!" she said. "Is it food?" Daddy laughed. "No, silly. A spider is an animal too. It lives outside." The spider sat very still. "Are we safe?" Emily asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "The window keeps us safe. The spider cannot get in."

Daddy knocked on the window, tap tap. The spider jumped. Then it crawled away. "Bye bye, spider," said Emily. She waved her banana at it.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Bennett's house. "How long?" Bennett asked. "One whole week," said Grandpa. "That is seven sleeps." Mom helped Bennett make a paper chain. It had seven red links. Each night, they would tear one off.

In the morning, they went to the market. "Let's try the bread stand," said Grandpa. They got there early. The bread was still warm and fresh. Later they passed a tank with a turtle. The turtle hid in its shell. Bennett clapped, and it hid more. "Too loud," Bennett said. He whispered, and the turtle peeked out. "It comes out because I am quiet," Bennett said. Grandpa nodded.

Each night they tore one link off. One link fell, then two, then three. On the last night, one link was left. Bennett held Grandpa's hand. "Only one more sleep," he said. Grandpa smiled. "Then I will come back soon." Bennett tore the last red link, and they waved it together like a tiny flag.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Today was Ayla's first day of school. She ran into the big cafeteria with her lunchbox. It was winter, so Mom had packed warm soup.

Ayla did not know where to sit. She counted the long tables. One table. Two tables. Three tables. Then she saw a little card on table four. The card said AYLA. "That is my name!" she said. She sat down fast.

Her friend Ben sat across from her. He had warm soup too. Ayla opened her lunchbox. "Smelly broccoli!" she said with a giggle. Ben laughed. Then came the surprise. He opened his box and he had smelly broccoli too!

Ayla clapped her hands. "We are the same!" she said. She took a big bite and said, "I know where my seat is. It has my name!" Ben held up his broccoli. "Broccoli friends!" he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Sarah sat at the big table. She wanted to make a paper garden. She had green paper and red paper and little yellow flowers.

Mama gave her the glue. "Just a little bit," said Mama. Sarah squeezed the bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. The glue came out in a big puddle. It was white and wet and cold on her fingers. She pressed a flower down. The flower slid away. She pressed it again. It slid again.

"Oh no," said Sarah. The paper got soft and yucky. A hole grew where the glue sat. Too much glue made the paper wet. The wet paper tore.

Mama sat down next to her. "We can fix it," said Mama. She gave Sarah a new green paper. "Try one little dot." Sarah made one small dot of glue. She pressed a flower on it. She counted to five. The flower stayed. It did not slide at all.

Sarah made dot after dot. The red tulip stayed. The yellow daisies stayed. Her garden filled up with flowers. "Little dots hold," said Sarah. Mama smiled and hung the garden on the fridge.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Billie ran to the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Billie wore her sun hat. "Why do I need this hat?" she asked. Her mother smiled and pointed up. "The sun is hot," she said. Billie felt her hat keep the sun off her head. "My hat stops the sun!" she said.

Then the wind came. It was a windy day now. The wind grabbed Billie's hat. Off it flew! The hat rolled down the street. "Come back!" Billie shouted. She ran and ran. The wind pushed the hat again. But then the hat hit a bush and stopped. Billie picked it up. "The wind blew my hat because it is light," she said. She held it tight with both hands.

Big clouds came next. Drip, drop. Rain fell. It was a rainy day. Billie had no raincoat. Her mother opened a big umbrella. They stood under it together. Billie put out one hand. Rain tapped her fingers. "The rain can't reach me here!" she said. The rain got the road all wet and shiny.

The bus came at last. Billie climbed up the big steps. She looked out the window. Way up on the hills, she saw white. "What is that?" she asked. Her mother said, "That is snow." Snowy places need thick, warm coats. Billie hugged her own warm coat. "One day I will play in the snow!" she said. The bus went beep, and off they drove.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Maeve sat on the big bus with her grandma. She held her bunny. The bus went bump. The bunny fell down. Maeve could not see it anywhere.

"Oh no," said Maeve. "Bunny is lost."

Grandma held her hand. "Let's look where bunny fell," she said. "Things fall down, and then they stay close." Maeve looked under the seat. She saw something soft. It was bunny! The bus went bump again, and bunny slid a little more. "The bus moves bunny," said Maeve. "Because the floor is not straight." She caught bunny and hugged him tight.

"Good looking," said Grandma. "Bunny is safe now." Maeve smiled. She held bunny all the way home.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Ryan wore his blue sweater to daycare. Outside the window, gray clouds sat low in the sky. Little flakes of snow began to fall.

"Time to clean up," said Miss Kim. Ryan looked for his ten red blocks. He could only see a few. He wanted all ten for his tall tower.

Ryan began to count. "One, two, three." Only three blocks sat on the rug. He looked under the table. "Four, five, six." Three more blocks were hiding there. He looked in the toy box. "Seven, eight, nine." Now he had nine.

One block was still lost. Ryan sang his counting song, the one from circle time. "Eight, nine, ten." He walked slowly around the rug as he sang. There, by the doll house, was block ten.

"The song helps me look," Ryan said. He stacked all ten blocks up, up, up. Outside, the snow fell soft and white.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Lily wants to paint a letter for Mom. It is school time, and the paint table is open.

She takes a big paper. It is as big as her arms. Sam takes a small paper. It is as small as his hand. They paint together. Lily makes red hearts. The paint feels slimy on her fingers. She says, "Big and small, slimy paint, here we go."

Lily wants to put her letter in her bag. But the paint is wet. It will smush. Teacher says, "Let's put them in the sun." The sun is hot. The shade under the tree is cold. Lily puts her letter in the hot sun. Sam puts his in the shade.

A snail walks by. It goes slow. A boy runs fast to the swings. Lily waits. She counts, "One, two, three." Her big letter is still wet. Sam's small letter is dry. She looks and looks. Then she sees it. "Small dries first," she says. "Big needs more sun."

She counts to ten. At ten, her letter is dry. The hearts shine red. Lily holds it up high. "My letter for Mom," she says. "Big and dry and all done."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Gabriel wanted to roll his red ball to the kitchen. He gave it a big push. The ball was a circle, so it rolled fast. It rolled under the table. "Come back!" said Gabriel. He reached out his arm. His arm was too short. He could not catch the ball.

Gabriel looked around for help. He found a square block. He pushed the square block with one finger. It did not roll. "Silly block," said Gabriel. "You are too flat on the bottom." Then he found his triangle hat and his rectangle book. He pushed them too. They just slid. "No, no," he laughed.

Only circles can roll. Gabriel grabbed his long rectangle ruler. He poked it under the table. The ball popped out. "I catch you!" said Gabriel. Then Mama clapped from the doorway. "My shape boy!"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Madison went to the library with her dad. The floor by the door was wet and slippery, so she walked slowly. She saw a big rug with ten ducks on it.

A lady sat down to sing. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. "Once I caught a fish alive." Madison clapped. She wanted to sing too. But when the song ended, her mouth felt mixed up. What came after five? She had said the words her own way at home. She said, "One, two, five, nine, six." The lady smiled, but the song did not sound right.

Madison thought hard. Why did the song sound wrong? She asked her dad, "Did I say them wrong?" He said, "Try again. Listen first." The lady sang again. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words came out in the same order every time. That was why the song worked!

Madison followed the words with her finger, duck by duck. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." It sounded right now. "The numbers go in a line," she said. "Just like ducks at the park." She sang it all by herself, and the lady gave her a gold star sticker.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story: Charlotte wants to paint with her big brother Leo. He is at the table with the red pot. "My turn first," says Leo. "Then you." Charlotte waits. She taps her toes. She counts one cup, two cups, three cups on the table. Leo paints a red bee. "Your turn now," he says. He gives her the red pot. Charlotte paints a red flower. Then Leo wants red again. "But it is my turn," says Charlotte. "You had it first. Now it is mine." Mom nods from the sink. "Charlotte is right," says Mom. "We take turns. That is fair." Leo thinks, then smiles. "Okay. You paint one more bee. Then I go." Charlotte paints a slow, sleepy bee. "This bee is asleep," she laughs. Leo claps. "Good job, Charlotte. Your turn is fun too."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sarah wanted to wash her hands all by herself. She stood on her old step stool at the sink. Dad stood near the door.

Sarah turned the tap. Hot water came out. Steam went up, up, up. Sarah pulled her hands back fast.

"The water is hot," Sarah said. "Hot water can hurt me." She turned the tap the other way. Now the water felt cool and nice.

Dad smiled. "Good thinking, Sarah," he said.

Sarah washed her hands with soap. Bubbles grew big and white. She splashed a little. Then she saw Dad's razor on the sink.

"What is that?" Sarah asked.

"That is a razor," Dad said. "It is sharp. It can cut you. Little hands do not touch it."

Sarah nodded. She kept her hands in the bubbles. She did not touch the razor.

Then Sarah saw the water rising in the sink. She turned the tap off. The water stopped. "I did it," she said. "I turned it off all by myself."

She jumped down from her stool. She held Dad's hand. They walked out of the bathroom together.

"Wash hands, no touching sharp things," Sarah said.

Dad laughed. "You are a big helper now," he said.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Emilia took a warm bath. The water smelled like soap. Then Mama lifted her out. Emilia was dripping wet.

Soon Emilia shivered. Her arms felt cold. "Why am I cold?" she asked. Mama gave her a soft towel. Emilia rubbed her arms and her legs. The drops went into the towel. Warm came back! "Wet makes me cold," said Emilia. "Dry makes me warm."

Then Emilia put on her pajamas. One arm, then the other. She pulled them up all by herself. "I did it!" she said.

Papa set his phone on the table. It buzzed. Grandma was calling. Emilia waved hello at the screen. Then the phone went quiet. Baby Tom was asleep, so they all whispered. Emilia ate her bread. Then she yawned a big yawn. Mama picked her up and carried her to bed.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Elijah sat in the big salon chair. The chair was too tall for him. Papa gave him a little boost. A man named Sam put a dark cape on Elijah. The cape was dark like night. Elijah wanted to look like Papa. Papa had short hair.

Sam turned on the buzzer. It made a funny sound. Bzzz, bzzz. Elijah giggled. Sam cut the hair on top. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the dark cape. "Look, Papa! My hair fell!" said Elijah. Sam smiled. "The buzzer makes it fall," said Elijah. "The buzzer does the work!"

Sam held up a mirror. Elijah saw a boy with short hair. The boy looked just like a little Papa. Elijah patted his head. "All gone!" he said. Sam laughed and gave him a sticker shaped like a star.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Zoey wanted a special snack. She got her little bowl and ten crackers. She put them on the table, one by one.

Daddy said, "Let's count them first." Zoey touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, six." Daddy smiled. "Wait. What comes after four?" Zoey looked at her hand. She held up five fingers. "Five comes after four!" She counted again, slow and patient. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten crackers, all in a line.

Zoey ate one cracker. She counted the rest. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Nine now! Daddy said, "You ate one, so now there are nine." Zoey laughed. "One went in my tummy!" She drew a picture of her ten crackers. At the top she wrote wiggly marks. "Ten crackers," she said. "One, two, three, all the way to ten."

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Grace stood in the school hallway. Her backpack was on. Her shoes were new. This was her very first day.

"Where does my backpack go?" she asked. The hallway had many hooks. A boy named Tom put his backpack on a hook. Then a girl put hers on a hook too. Grace did not know which hook was hers. She began to freeze like a small statue.

Then she saw it. A little card on one hook. It had her name on it. Grace. "That is my hook," she said. "My name is on it!" She hung her backpack there. It did not fall down. It stayed because the hook held it.

Tom looked at her. "Last one to the classroom is a silly goose!" he said.

"Not me!" said Grace. She ran past Tom. Outside the window, the street was sunny. Grace laughed all the way to her classroom.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Milan wanted to find the ice cream cart at the park. He could not see it anywhere. He looked with his eyes. He saw swings and a big slide. No ice cream cart.

Then he stopped and stood very still. He heard a little bell with his ears. Ding, ding! Was that the ice cream man? Milan sniffed with his nose. The air smelled sweet, like vanilla. His mouth watered, and he could almost taste it on his tongue. He ran toward the sound. The bell rang louder and louder. There it was! The cart was hiding behind a big tree. "How did you find me?" the ice cream man asked. "My ears heard your bell," said Milan. "The bell rings, so I can hear it. That is how I know where you are."

Milan got a vanilla cone. It felt cold on his fingers. "You are a lucky boy," said the ice cream man. "A lucky elephant likes vanilla too," he laughed, and pointed at a toy elephant on his cart. Milan licked his cone and smiled. His eyes, ears, nose, tongue and fingers had all helped him today. "One more thing," said the man. He rang the bell right by Milan's ear. Ding! "Now your tongue can taste the sweet, and your ears can hear the ring," he said. Milan took one more big lick.
